prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "MICRON TECHNOLOGY INC" (ticker MU), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "MU", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?

Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Micron Technology, Inc.
result.industry: Semiconductors: memory and storage chips (DRAM, HBM, NAND)
markets: DRAM (data-center server memory, PC and smartphone memory)

mission.source: Micron publishes its vision as "transform how the world uses information to enrich life for all" (company website); its FY2026 10-K overview uses the phrase "accelerating intelligence to enrich life for all"; an exact official mission wording could not be confirmed
mission.plain: Make the memory chips that let computers and AI store and use information faster, to make life better for everyone.

about.plain: Micron makes memory chips, the parts of a computer that remember things. Some memory holds what a computer is working on right now (DRAM), and some keeps your photos and files even when the power is off (NAND flash). Its newest, most wanted chips are stacks of super-fast memory that sit next to AI chips. It is the only big US-based company that makes these memory chips.
about.customers: Makers of AI chips and servers, big cloud companies, and makers of phones, PCs and cars buy its chips.
about.everyday: The memory inside many smartphones, laptops (Crucial-brand upgrades) and the AI servers that run chatbots comes from Micron.

money.part: Memory for cloud and AI data centers
money.plain: HBM and high-capacity DRAM for hyperscale clouds and AI chips
server DRAM modules and data-center SSDs
memory and storage chips for smartphones and computers
tough memory chips for cars, machines and devices
custom stacked memory for NVIDIA and other AI accelerators

result.summary: Micron has a real but cyclical advantage: it is one of only three companies in the world (with Samsung and SK hynix) that can make leading-edge DRAM and HBM at scale, a position protected by tens of billions of dollars of fabs and decades of process know-how. That oligopoly has delivered record FY2026 results (revenue $133.2B, 81% gross margin), but memory is a commodity-like product whose prices swing with supply, so its moat is narrower than its current profits suggest.

pricingPower.evidence: In the AI-driven memory shortage revenue rose from $37.4B in FY2025 to $133.2B in FY2026 and gross margin from about 40% to 81%, driven mainly by price; but in the FY2023 downturn prices collapsed and revenue fell 49% to $15.5B with a negative gross margin, showing pricing is set by industry supply rather than by Micron.

moats.evidence: Memory is bought on specifications and qualification, not brand; the Crucial consumer brand is small and Micron holds a large patent portfolio but rivals have equivalent ones.

HBM and server DRAM must be qualified for each customer platform (e.g. NVIDIA's GPUs) over many months, and HBM supply is negotiated in annual contracts, but customers deliberately dual- or triple-source.
A memory chip is not more valuable because others use the same supplier.
Micron is the world's third-largest DRAM maker (22.4% of DRAM revenue in 4Q25, TrendForce) and spent $27.4B of net capex in FY2026; new entrants cannot match the scale or yields of the three leaders.

Leading-edge DRAM is a three-player oligopoly (Samsung, SK hynix, Micron hold over 90% of revenue) because each new fab costs tens of billions, leaving room for few suppliers; China's CXMT is the main challenger.
Micron competes with the same business model as Samsung and SK hynix.
Micron was first to ship 1-beta and 1-gamma DRAM nodes and its HBM3E claimed lower power than rivals, know-how built over 40+ years; but Samsung and SK hynix have comparable process skills.
It is the only large US-headquartered memory maker, giving it preferred access to CHIPS Act funding and US government support for its Idaho and New York fabs, but no exclusive technology.

customers.evidence: Micron is a qualified HBM supplier to NVIDIA and other AI-chip makers and says much of its HBM output is sold out under annual contracts, but buyers are price-driven and spread purchases across Samsung, SK hynix and Micron.

talent.evidence: About 61,000 employees (FY2026 10-K) in the US, Asia and Europe; strong engineering reputation in Boise and Singapore, but memory has historically had lower pay and prestige than leading logic and AI chip designers, and it has cut staff in downturns.

product.evidence: Micron has led node transitions (first to ship 1-beta and 1-gamma DRAM, 232- and 276-layer NAND) and its HBM3E/HBM4 are qualified in NVIDIA platforms; in HBM it held about 21% share in Q3 2025 versus SK hynix's 57% (Counterpoint), so it is competitive rather than the clear leader.

competitors.name: SK hynix
competitors.note: DRAM and HBM leader (about 57% of HBM in Q3 2025) and NAND via Solidigm; financial figures in estimates are estimates converted from KRW.

competitors.name: Samsung Electronics
competitors.note: Largest memory maker in DRAM (36% in 4Q25) and NAND (28%), regaining HBM share; financial figures are estimates for the whole company converted from KRW.

competitors.name: ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT)
competitors.note: Chinese state-backed DRAM maker (about 5% of DRAM in Q3 2025, Counterpoint) growing in DDR4/DDR5 and LPDDR for Chinese customers.

competitors.name: Sandisk
competitors.note: NAND flash and SSDs (12.8% of NAND revenue in 4Q25), spun off from Western Digital in 2025.

competitors.name: Kioxia
competitors.note: NAND flash and enterprise SSDs (14.1% of NAND in 4Q25); financial figures are estimates converted from JPY.

competitors.name: Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC)
competitors.note: Chinese NAND maker competing in consumer and Chinese SSD markets despite US export restrictions.

competitors.name: Nanya Technology
competitors.note: Taiwanese specialty and legacy DRAM (about 2% of DRAM).

competitors.name: Winbond Electronics
competitors.note: Specialty DRAM and NOR/NAND flash for embedded, automotive and industrial uses.

competitors.name: Kingston Technology
competitors.note: Private memory-module and SSD brand competing with Micron's Crucial consumer products (buys chips from memory makers).

threats: Memory price cycle: new fab capacity from Samsung, SK hynix and Micron itself could flip today's shortage into oversupply, as in FY2023 when revenue fell 49% and gross margin turned negative.
SK hynix's lead in HBM (about 57% share) and Samsung's HBM comeback could squeeze Micron's share and pricing in AI memory.
Chinese makers CXMT (DRAM) and YMTC (NAND), backed by the state, adding capacity in mainstream products.
Customer concentration in AI: a slowdown in hyperscaler or NVIDIA spending would hit HBM and data-center demand.
Geopolitics: China's 2023 ban on Micron in critical infrastructure, export controls and Taiwan/Japan fab exposure.
Heavy capex for new US fabs in Idaho and New York raises fixed costs going into any downturn.

ceo.name: Sanjay Mehrotra
ceo.background: Electrical engineer (B.S. and M.S. in EECS, UC Berkeley; Stanford executive program); co-founded SanDisk in 1988 and was its CEO 2011-2016

c1.evidence: Micron is one of only three leaders in AI memory (HBM), a fast-growing market, but it ranks third in DRAM (22.4% in 4Q25) and in HBM (about 21% vs SK hynix's 57%).

c2.evidence: Customers choose Micron for power-efficient HBM3E/HBM4, leading-edge 1-gamma DRAM and as the only US-based supplier, but Samsung and SK hynix can match most of these advantages, so it is hard to copy only for new entrants.

c3.evidence: Ordinary people rarely know Micron (they may know its Crucial brand), and it is not the default leader in memory, a position held by Samsung in DRAM/NAND and SK hynix in HBM.

c4.evidence: Micron's vision to "transform how the world uses information to enrich life for all" is emphasised in its reports, but management is judged mainly on cycle-driven financial results rather than a purpose-led mission.

c6.evidence: “memory chips, cyclical, American, AI winner”: investors and tech readers see it mostly positively as a key AI supplier, while the wider public largely does not know the name.

c7.evidence: WSTS-cited data put memory chip sales at $230B in 2025 with forecasts near $800B for 2026, driven by the secular AI build-out that needs ever more HBM and server DRAM.

c8.evidence: It can grow into custom HBM (HBM4E base dies), CXL memory expansion and AI PCs/phones, but it stays within memory and storage rather than moving into wholly new markets.

m1.evidence: Mehrotra says "AI is becoming Super Intelligence, and memory enhances this intelligence" and pushed Micron early into HBM3E, but his vision is focused on memory roadmaps rather than reshaping industries.

m2.evidence: As a SanDisk co-founder he brings founder-style long-term thinking, committing about $200B to US manufacturing and R&D, but he is a hired CEO at Micron rather than its founder.

m4.evidence: There is little public evidence either way about a servant-leadership style; Micron has cut staff in downturns (such as the 2022-23 memory slump) and talks mainly about customers and technology.

m5.evidence: Under Mehrotra Micron moved from laggard to node leader (first to 1-alpha, 1-beta and 1-gamma DRAM) and built HBM from scratch, though its culture is not widely seen as distinctive.

m6.evidence: Mehrotra is an electrical engineer from UC Berkeley who holds patents in flash memory and is deeply involved in Micron's technology roadmap.

m7.evidence: No controversies are known and he supports STEM education and US manufacturing, but there is no clear public record of mission beyond the business.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Sanjay Mehrotra at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar university could be found.

m8b.evidence: Mehrotra is a low-profile, technical executive rather than a celebrity CEO.

m9.evidence: Since 2017 he has lifted Micron to record FY2026 revenue of $133.2B and net income of $85.0B, regained technology leadership and won HBM qualification at NVIDIA.

m10.evidence: Micron cuts capex and costs sharply in downturns (e.g. FY2023 wafer-start and staff cuts), but it is not known for a frugal culture.

c10.evidence: Its memory sits in billions of phones, PCs, cars and the AI servers behind chatbots, but it is a hidden component rather than a product that directly changes lives.

p2.evidence: Making 1-gamma DRAM and 12-high HBM stacks needs EUV lithography, nanometre-scale processes and multi-billion-dollar fabs, and only three companies can do it at scale; it is essential to AI computing.

f1.evidence: Revenue fell 49% in FY2023 (to $15.5B from $30.8B) before rising to $25.1B, $37.4B and $133.2B in FY2024-FY2026.

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from 37.6% in FY2021 to 80.7% in FY2026 and operating margin from 22.7% to 74.6%, but with a deep loss in FY2023 (operating margin -37%), so the rise is cyclical rather than steady.

f3.evidence: At September 3, 2026 debt was $5.2B against $43.4B of cash and short-term investments (plus $30.0B long-term investments) and FY2026 operating cash flow of $89.7B, with positive equity.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $6.3B in FY2021 to $99.3B in FY2026 and operating cash flow reached $89.7B (vs $17.5B in FY2025), but both fell sharply in FY2023.

v1.evidence: Memory is largely interchangeable; SK hynix is seen as the HBM leader and Samsung as the volume leader, so there is no everyday reason to pick Micron over every alternative.

v2.evidence: Micron is a large employer with about 61,000 staff, but no top-tier employer ranking for it could be confirmed.

c5.evidence: If Micron vanished, AI chip makers, cloud providers and phone and car makers would face shortages and higher memory prices, and the US would lose its only big memory maker, though Samsung and SK hynix could eventually fill the gap.
